decisions.note: Not a use of the mode. src/krux/krux_settings.py:425 defines MODE_NAMES = {ucryptolib.MODE_ECB: "AES-ECB", ...}, a mapping from mode constant to the label shown in the settings menu, so the device can print which format a user picked. No key, no plaintext and no call to ucryptolib.aes appears here. The design decision this finding is really about is in src/krux/kef.py and is decided separately below; counting it twice would report one choice as two problems.

Real and deliberate: src/krux/kef.py defines the Krux Encrypted Format, and of its eleven versions four are ECB — version 0 "AES-ECB v1" (released 2023.08 for BIP-39 entropy), 5 "AES-ECB", 6 "AES-ECB +p" and 7 "AES-ECB +c". So a user can store an encrypted mnemonic under ECB, and old backups already are. Reported at medium rather than high, because the usual reasons for calling ECB high do not all hold here and saying so is the point of a review. Every version carries an `auth` field sizing an authentication tag, so integrity is not left to the mode; GCM versions 20 and 21 exist in the same table; and the maintainers document the actual hazard themselves, version 6 reading "safe padding: for mid-sized plaintext w/o duplicate blocks" and 7 "may compact otherwise duplicate blocks". For the intended payload — one or two blocks of high-entropy mnemonic — ECB's block-repetition leak has little to bite on. What remains true, and is the actionable half: versions 6 and 7 exist precisely for larger plaintext, which is where duplicate blocks become possible, and ECB there leaks structure that CTR or GCM would not. The recommendation is not "remove ECB" (that would orphan 2023 backups) but to keep the ECB versions for decryption of old backups and stop offering them for new ones.

The iteration count is a protocol constant, not a hardening parameter. vendor/embit/src/embit/slip39.py:51 calls hashlib.pbkdf2_hmac("sha256", i + passphrase, salt + right, 2500 << exponent, half) inside _crypt, which is SLIP-39's four-round Feistel construction: 2500 per round times four rounds is the specification's base iteration count of 10000, and `exponent` is SLIP-39's own iteration-exponent field, which a share carries so that any implementation can reproduce it. Raising it to OWASP's 600,000 — the rule's recommendation, which is correct guidance for password storage — would produce shares that no other SLIP-39 implementation could read, and would therefore destroy the interoperability that makes a backup standard worth using. The rule is right that 2500 is low for a password; it is the wrong question for a protocol constant. Worth separating from a real concern: SLIP-39's security rests on the share secret, not on the passphrase being hard to guess, so the iteration count is not what protects a strong share.

Correct, and this is the finding the audit exists to produce. 53 of the 98 inventory rows are ECDSA and they span the whole chain: src/krux/key.py:255 calls secp256k1.ecdsa_sign_recoverable through embit, which dispatches in vendor/embit/src/embit/util/secp256k1.py either to ctypes_secp256k1.py (the C library) or to py_secp256k1.py (a pure-Python fallback), and the C library itself is vendored again at vendor/embit/secp256k1/secp256k1-zkp/. Every spend this device authorises is a discrete-log signature over secp256k1, so Shor applies to the signing path in full. Forward-only rather than retroactive: a signature already published cannot be made more secret, but a public key that has been seen on chain can be attacked the day a CRQC exists, which is why address reuse is the behaviour worth changing before the scheme does.

Correct. Seven rows, in vendor/embit/src/embit/util/secp256k1.py:33 and ctypes_secp256k1.py:287 and in the vendored library's own schnorrsig module. Taproot spends therefore sit in the same class as ECDSA ones: BIP-340 changes the signature's shape, not the hardness assumption it rests on.

Correct but narrow, and the narrowness is worth recording so nobody reads this as four more rows of spending exposure. All four are Liquid, not Bitcoin: vendor/embit/src/embit/liquid/pset.py:101 and liquid/transaction.py:90 call secp256k1.pedersen_commit for confidential-transaction value commitments, via util/secp256k1.py:51 and ctypes_secp256k1.py:949. The property at risk is the commitment's *binding*, which rests on the discrete log, so a CRQC could forge a value commitment; the *hiding* property is information-theoretic and no quantum computer touches it. A post-quantum signature standard does not fix this — it needs a different commitment scheme — and it only matters to users who spend Liquid assets.

Kept rather than dismissed. The rule could not classify the role for five files, and that is honest: the anchor is src/krux/key.py:252-255, where the import of embit.util.secp256k1 and the call to ecdsa_sign_recoverable sit together, so the role is in fact transaction signing and the surrounding rows say so. Left as "role not determined" in the report because the classifier's own confidence should not be overwritten by the analyst's reading of the same lines; the decision records the reading instead.

Correct as a single non-runtime summary, and it is the one thing in this audit that the submodule fix made worse before a second fix made it right. vendor/embit/poetry.lock pins 55 packages and every one of them is `optional = true` behind `markers = 'extra == "dev"'`, so embit has no unconditional runtime dependencies at all: the lock file describes how embit is developed and documented, not what it ships. Read by Poetry groups alone they all appeared to be runtime — Poetry 2 files extras under the main group — and this repository briefly reported one critical and sixteen high advisories, eleven of them virtualenv, for a device that runs MicroPython on a K210 and pip-installs nothing. The parser now treats an optional package gated behind a development-shaped extra as non-runtime. Nothing in this group reaches the firmware.

findings.title: Quantum-vulnerable ECDSA: transaction and message signing (39 file(s))
findings.description: 296 reference(s) to ECDSA across 39 file(s), e.g. vendor/embit/secp256k1/secp256k1-zkp/contrib/lax_der_parsing.c:11. Role, judged from paths, function names and nearby code: transaction and message signing. A CRQC derives the private key from a public key that is already known (on chain after the first spend, in reused addresses): funds and approvals controlled by these keys need a migration path.
findings.impact: Long-term risk depends on what the algorithm protects: signatures (authenticity until migration) or key exchange/encryption (retroactive decryption of recorded data).
findings.recommendation: Follow each chain's post-quantum roadmap, avoid public-key reuse, and keep signers ready to add post-quantum signature schemes as chains adopt them.
findings.limitations: This is a forward-looking risk that depends on the arrival of a cryptographically relevant quantum computer (CRQC). No such computer is publicly known to exist today; the timeline is uncertain. It is not a present-day exploitable vulnerability. Heuristic pattern match on source text without data-flow analysis. The usage context (security-relevant or not) must be confirmed manually; treat as preliminary.

triage.note: Correct, and this is the finding the audit exists to produce. 53 of the 98 inventory rows are ECDSA and they span the whole chain: src/krux/key.py:255 calls secp256k1.ecdsa_sign_recoverable through embit, which dispatches in vendor/embit/src/embit/util/secp256k1.py either to ctypes_secp256k1.py (the C library) or to py_secp256k1.py (a pure-Python fallback), and the C library itself is vendored again at vendor/embit/secp256k1/secp256k1-zkp/. Every spend this device authorises is a discrete-log signature over secp256k1, so Shor applies to the signing path in full. Forward-only rather than retroactive: a signature already published cannot be made more secret, but a public key that has been seen on chain can be attacked the day a CRQC exists, which is why address reuse is the behaviour worth changing before the scheme does.

Role, judged from paths, function names and nearby code: threshold signing and MPC protocols. Paillier, Pedersen commitments and the discrete-logarithm proofs inside threshold ECDSA and EdDSA protocols all fall to Shor's algorithm; a post-quantum threshold scheme is a protocol change, not a parameter change.

findings.limitations: This is a forward-looking risk that depends on the arrival of a cryptographically relevant quantum computer (CRQC). triage.note: Correct but narrow, and the narrowness is worth recording so nobody reads this as four more rows of spending exposure. All four are Liquid, not Bitcoin: vendor/embit/src/embit/liquid/pset.py:101 and liquid/transaction.py:90 call secp256k1.pedersen_commit for confidential-transaction value commitments, via util/secp256k1.py:51 and ctypes_secp256k1.py:949. The property at risk is the commitment's *binding*, which rests on the discrete log, so a CRQC could forge a value commitment; the *hiding* property is information-theoretic and no quantum computer touches it. A post-quantum signature standard does not fix this — it needs a different commitment scheme — and it only matters to users who spend Liquid assets.

findings.title: ECB block-cipher mode used in src/krux/kef.py
findings.description: 8 usage(s) of ECB mode (first at line 30).
findings.impact: ECB reveals patterns in encrypted data and provides no integrity.
findings.recommendation: Use an AEAD mode (GCM) with unique nonces.
findings.retest: Re-scan the source and review the call sites listed in the evidence.
findings.limitations: Heuristic pattern match on source text without data-flow analysis. The usage context (security-relevant or not) must be confirmed manually; treat as preliminary.
findings.method: Regular-expression matching of language-specific API patterns.
findings.repro: Open line 30 in the supplied file src/krux/kef.py and inspect the quoted lines (see evidence).

triage.note: Real and deliberate: src/krux/kef.py defines the Krux Encrypted Format, and of its eleven versions four are ECB — version 0 "AES-ECB v1" (released 2023.08 for BIP-39 entropy), 5 "AES-ECB", 6 "AES-ECB +p" and 7 "AES-ECB +c". So a user can store an encrypted mnemonic under ECB, and old backups already are. Reported at medium rather than high, because the usual reasons for calling ECB high do not all hold here and saying so is the point of a review. Every version carries an `auth` field sizing an authentication tag, so integrity is not left to the mode; GCM versions 20 and 21 exist in the same table; and the maintainers document the actual hazard themselves, version 6 reading "safe padding: for mid-sized plaintext w/o duplicate blocks" and 7 "may compact otherwise duplicate blocks". For the intended payload — one or two blocks of high-entropy mnemonic — ECB's block-repetition leak has little to bite on. What remains true, and is the actionable half: versions 6 and 7 exist precisely for larger plaintext, which is where duplicate blocks become possible, and ECB there leaks structure that CTR or GCM would not. The recommendation is not "remove ECB" (that would orphan 2023 backups) but to keep the ECB versions for decryption of old backups and stop offering them for new ones.

findings.title: Low PBKDF2 iteration count (2500) in vendor/embit/src/embit/slip39.py
findings.impact: Low iteration counts make offline password guessing cheaper.
findings.recommendation: Follow current OWASP Password Storage guidance (e.g. 600,000 iterations for PBKDF2-HMAC-SHA256) or use Argon2id.
findings.retest: Re-scan the source and review the call sites listed in the evidence.

findings.repro: Open line 51 in the supplied file vendor/embit/src/embit/slip39.py and inspect the quoted lines (see evidence).

triage.note: The iteration count is a protocol constant, not a hardening parameter. vendor/embit/src/embit/slip39.py:51 calls hashlib.pbkdf2_hmac("sha256", i + passphrase, salt + right, 2500 << exponent, half) inside _crypt, which is SLIP-39's four-round Feistel construction: 2500 per round times four rounds is the specification's base iteration count of 10000, and `exponent` is SLIP-39's own iteration-exponent field, which a share carries so that any implementation can reproduce it. Raising it to OWASP's 600,000 — the rule's recommendation, which is correct guidance for password storage — would produce shares that no other SLIP-39 implementation could read, and would therefore destroy the interoperability that makes a backup standard worth using. The rule is right that 2500 is low for a password; it is the wrong question for a protocol constant. Worth separating from a real concern: SLIP-39's security rests on the share secret, not on the passphrase being hard to guess, so the iteration count is not what protects a strong share.

findings.description: OSV.dev lists 40 advisories (17 rated high or critical) for 8 PyPI package(s) that only development or build tooling pulls in (vendor/embit/poetry.lock): e.g. black@26.3.1 [dev]: GHSA-cg8m-r9f2-5wm2; certifi@2026.2.25 [dev]: GHSA-6q48-6c7w-9gw2; filelock@3.25.2 [dev]: GHSA-567q-5qvw-pf92, GHSA-69hj-f68j-2879, GHSA-8mx5-7m5m-r77g, GHSA-9vhv-jxww-xfm5, GHSA-cwqr-hh33-gh44, GHSA-fq56-3cx3-fjxp, GHSA-j8f7-rjxc-mr56, GHSA-rfpc-qcw5-3pc4, GHSA-v4x8-3wr5-3wq8; idna@3.11 [dev]: GHSA-65pc-fj4g-8rjx; mkdocs-material@9.7.6 [dev]: GHSA-xvg9-69gf-fjrf. The manifests mark them as such (devDependencies, "dev": true in package-lock.json, pnpm importers sections, [dev-dependencies]/[build-dependencies] reached through Cargo.lock, or — for yarn.lock, which records no scope at all — package.json reached through the lock graph), so they are not part of what ships.
findings.impact: They do not reach users of the product. They can affect developer machines and CI (supply chain): a compromised or vulnerable tool can tamper with builds.
findings.recommendation: Update the tooling during routine maintenance; prioritise packages that run in CI with secrets or that produce release artefacts.
findings.retest: Re-run the dependency scan after updating.
findings.limitations: Advisory data comes from OSV.dev at the recorded time. Scopes come from the manifests; a registry crate's own build dependencies cannot be told apart in Cargo.lock, so the runtime set may be larger than reality, never smaller.
findings.method: OSV.dev querybatch lookup of exact versions; scope from devDependencies, package-lock.json dev flags, pnpm importers sections, the Cargo.lock graph rooted at the Cargo.toml tables, and — for yarn.lock, which records no scope — the lock graph walked from package.json. Where a runtime requirement cannot be resolved in a lock, that lock is left unclassified rather than risking a package being set aside wrongly.
findings.repro: Look the packages listed in the evidence up at https://osv.dev and check their scope in vendor/embit/poetry.lock.

triage.note: Correct as a single non-runtime summary, and it is the one thing in this audit that the submodule fix made worse before a second fix made it right. vendor/embit/poetry.lock pins 55 packages and every one of them is `optional = true` behind `markers = 'extra == "dev"'`, so embit has no unconditional runtime dependencies at all: the lock file describes how embit is developed and documented, not what it ships. Read by Poetry groups alone they all appeared to be runtime — Poetry 2 files extras under the main group — and this repository briefly reported one critical and sixteen high advisories, eleven of them virtualenv, for a device that runs MicroPython on a K210 and pip-installs nothing. The parser now treats an optional package gated behind a development-shaped extra as non-runtime. Nothing in this group reaches the firmware.

quantum_algorithms.name: Shor's algorithm — elliptic-curve discrete logarithms
quantum_algorithms.model_label: Q1: quantum computation offline, classical access to the victim
quantum_algorithms.audit: Elliptic-curve keys are expected to fall before RSA keys of comparable classical strength. On blockchains, coins whose public key is already on chain (reused addresses, pay-to-public-key and Taproot outputs) are exposed first; plan the move to post-quantum signatures and avoid key reuse in the meantime.
quantum_algorithms.practicality: 2026 estimates for a 256-bit curve: under 1,200 logical qubits and 90 million Toffoli gates, under half a million physical superconducting qubits running for minutes (Babbush et al.); 1,193 logical qubits with more gates (Chevignard–Fouque–Schrottenloher); P-256 in a few days on 26,000 neutral-atom qubits (Cain et al.). Scenarios under stated assumptions, not forecasts.

quantum_algorithms.name: Grover's algorithm — key search and preimages
quantum_algorithms.model_label: Q1: quantum computation offline, classical access to the victim
quantum_algorithms.audit: Not a break. 256-bit keys (AES-256, ChaCha20) keep a comfortable margin; AES-128 meets NIST category 1, while some authorities ask for 256-bit keys in quantum-resistant contexts (see the AES-128 entry). Prefer 256-bit keys for long-lived data; 256-bit hashes need no change for preimage resistance.
quantum_algorithms.practicality: The search is long and serial: NIST counts AES-128 key search as 2^170/MAXDEPTH quantum gates with MAXDEPTH between 2^40 and 2^96 and uses it as the yardstick of security category 1; a SHA-256 preimage was estimated at about 2^153.8 surface-code cycles on 2^12.6 logical qubits (Amy et al. 2016).

quantum_algorithms.name: Brassard–Høyer–Tapp — collision search
quantum_algorithms.model_label: Q1: quantum computation offline, classical access to the victim
quantum_algorithms.audit: 256-bit hashes (SHA-256, SHA3-256) remain adequate for collision resistance; 160-bit hashes are already weak classically (SHA-1 collisions are practical). Use 384/512-bit hashes where NIST categories 4–5 are required.
quantum_algorithms.practicality: Bernstein (2009) argued that, once hardware cost is counted, it is not cheaper than classical parallel collision search; NIST defines security category 2 by SHA3-256 collision search counted in classical gates (2^146).

quantum_algorithms.name: Simon's algorithm — superposition attacks on symmetric constructions
quantum_algorithms.model_label: Q2: superposition queries to the victim's keyed primitive
quantum_algorithms.audit: No action for ordinary deployments of AES-GCM or CBC-MAC — the attack model does not apply. Record it as a model assumption; see the offline variant for Even–Mansour-type designs.
quantum_algorithms.practicality: Requires quantum access to the device that holds the key. A server encrypting classical messages does not give it; the model matters for quantum networks and some obfuscation settings.
